frameworks.name: Revenue-Per-Square-Foot Service Line Prioritization
frameworks.definition: Identify the highest-revenue-per-square-foot service line, strip all lower-productivity offerings, and replicate the lean model across locations via franchising or organic growth.

frameworks.name: Three-Person Franchise Model
frameworks.definition: Minimal viable team structure: one manager handling morning/evening sales and service, plus two assistants rotating shifts, capable of $500k-$600k annual revenue at 50% margins.

claims.text: The hardest valuation to achieve is between $10M and $30M, because it is neither large enough for institutional investors nor small enough for individual high-net-worth buyers to care—a $100M exit is easier than a $25M exit (Alex Hormozi, service business portfolio context).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: The $10-30M band is too small to move the needle for large-checkbook acquirers yet too large for founder-level buyers to deploy at once.
bounded_by: Does not quantify the absolute difference in deal difficulty
Does not specify time to close or negotiation friction metrics

claims.text: High-service-based fitness and dance businesses are difficult to sell for a large multiple because they are talent-driven and dependent on the quality of instructors, coaches, and trainers—the business scales with people, not systems (Alex Hormozi, fitness service scaling).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: service-based gyms, dance studios, fitness facilities
claims.mechanism: Buyer perceives high execution risk because service quality depends on individual instructor talent, not repeatable systems or brand moat.
bounded_by: Does not apply to product-based fitness businesses (e.g., supplement brands, equipment sales)
Does not apply to systematized fitness franchises like Alloy that strip out high-touch service

claims.text: A buyer without business acumen (e.g., a doctor with capital but no operational experience) will acquire a talent-dependent service business at a discount ($10M with earn-out clauses and contingencies) rather than paying a premium—the buyer substitutes cash for knowledge, not valuation.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: buyer pool includes capital-rich but business-naive individuals

numbers.axis: exit valuation for talent-dependent service business

bounded_by: Does not apply to businesses with strong brand moat or systematized delivery

claims.text: Franchise and licensing models for service businesses are more valuable in M&A because they demonstrate scalability and reduce buyer perception of founder dependency—they are easier to monetize on exit than organic multi-location operations (Alex Hormozi, service business exits).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Franchise/licensing transfers brand, systems, and revenue model to third parties, demonstrating that founder dependency is not the binding constraint—the buyer sees repeatable operations.
bounded_by: Does not apply to capital-intensive businesses with unique supply chains
Does not guarantee higher exit price if the underlying service is not systematized

claims.text: Most fitness and dance studio owners who build multi-location operations end up piecemealing the exit rather than selling as a whole business—one location to a trainer, one to a customer, one to a competitor—because the systems do not transfer cleanly (Alex Hormozi, observed pattern across portfolio).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: multi-location service businesses without systematized replication
claims.mechanism: High personalization to individual location culture and instructor relationships prevents unified valuation; buyers prefer location-specific deals.
bounded_by: Does not apply to systematized models like Alloy that strip down to core repeatable unit
Does not quantify how many attempted full exits fail

claims.text: Revenue per square foot is the primary optimization lever for franchise replication in service businesses—identify the service line with the highest revenue-per-square-foot, maintain only that service, and eliminate or stop-promote everything else (Alex Hormozi, citing Alloy franchise strategy).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: complex multi-service model (PT, group classes, semi-private, merch, etc.)
claims.mechanism: Stripping down reduces operational complexity, enables lean staffing, improves replicability across locations, and raises margins.
bounded_by: Does not apply to bundled-service models where customer bundling is the value prop
Assumes revenue-per-square-foot is correlated with franchise scalability (not verified for all service types)

claims.text: At capacity (80% utilization on core programs in a dance or fitness business), facility space becomes the binding constraint to further revenue growth—adding daytime or tangential programs should be deprioritized until the core model is exhausted, to avoid complicating the replication blueprint (Alex Hormozi, dance studio scaling context).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: service business at 80%+ capacity on core offering
claims.mechanism: Adding complexity early makes the model harder to teach and replicate; standardizing on high-margin core service first creates a repeatable template.

anchors.value: market demand or conversion is binding constraint

bounded_by: Does not apply if adjacent daytime programs have independent demand sources
Assumes core program margins exceed adjacent programs (market-dependent)

claims.text: Alloy (Rick Mayo's semi-private training franchise) generates $500k-$600k annual revenue per location with 50% margins using a three-person team: one manager handling sales and morning/evening operations, and two assistants rotating morning/evening shifts—this model is cookie-cutterable across new locations (Alex Hormozi, citing Alloy franchise case).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Stripping out merch, PT, and large-group services to focus on highest-revenue-per-square-foot (semi-private) enables lean staffing and high margins.
bounded_by: Numbers reflect Alloy's specific model; margins and staffing vary by geography and service mix
Does not account for corporate overhead or marketing spend

claims.text: Rick Mayo, founder of Alloy, built a $4M single-facility business with multiple service lines (semi-private training, PT, large-group classes, smoothie bar, merch) and recognized that when he evaluated revenue per square foot across all units, semi-private training had the highest per-square-foot efficiency—when transitioning to a franchise model, he eliminated all other services and kept only semi-private (Alex Hormozi, Alloy case study).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Revenue-per-square-foot prioritization reveals which service line compounds better; cutting the rest reduces complexity and improves replicability.
bounded_by: Does not quantify revenue loss from cutting non-core services
Assumes semi-private remains profitable at reduced scale

examples.text: Rick Mayo built a $4M single-facility fitness business (6,000+ square feet) with a full service mix: semi-private training, one-on-one PT, large-group classes, smoothie bar, and merchandise. When he analyzed revenue per square foot across each service line, semi-private training had the highest efficiency. To launch a franchise model, he cut the lease commitment (still 6,000 sq ft) and stripped out everything except semi-private training, retaining all profitability while reducing complexity. The new 3-person team (manager plus two assistants on rotation) could replicate the $500k-$600k revenue model across new locations with 50% margins.

A dance studio owner with two locations and $2.7M revenue (aiming for $3M this year and $10M+ long-term) indicated willingness to add daytime programs and scale via organic growth or acquisition. Alex Hormozi advised against adding complexity at that stage, noting that until the core program hits 100% capacity, additional services dilute the replication blueprint. Instead, he recommended stripping the model to its highest-margin core (analogous to Alloy's semi-private focus) and building a franchise or licensing path, because multi-location organic scaling results in piecemeal exits rather than unified valuations.

practices.text: Strip down a multi-service business model to the single highest-revenue-per-square-foot service line before franchising or scaling to multiple locations—this reduces complexity and creates a repeatable, cookie-cutter template.

For dance, fitness, or service studios seeking a 10-20x valuation exit, prioritize franchising or licensing over organic multi-location growth, because organic growth leads to piecemeal exits (one location per buyer) rather than unified valuations.
When a service business reaches 80% capacity on core programs, pause expansion of ancillary services and instead focus on replicating the core model to new locations or franchise partners.
